turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

The offer:
- Base salary: $235,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($47,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,080,000, vesting over 4 years
- No sign-on bonus

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
**Short answer:** For a Google L6 PM, this is a solid offer that sits a bit above the middle of the market. But it probably isn't good enough to leave Meta for as it stands, and you shouldn't accept it without negotiating. You weren't looking and you're happy where you are, so your fallback is staying put. That's about the strongest negotiating position you can have.

## 1. What the offer is actually worth

Google offers now almost always use a front-loaded vesting schedule: 99% of Google's offers follow the 38/32/20/10 GSU vesting structure, and Google's GSUs vest monthly. Check with your recruiter that your grant follows it too. Assuming it does, and the bonus pays out at target:

| | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 | Year 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base + 20% bonus | $282K | $282K | $282K | $282K |
| GSUs | $410K | $346K | $216K | $108K |
| **Total (no refreshes)** | **$692K** | **$628K** | **$498K** | **$390K** |

The 4-year average is **$552K/year**. Year 1 looks great, but by year 4 the new-hire grant pays only $108K. Whether you keep earning $550K+ depends on refresh grants, and the recruiter told you those aren't guaranteed.

## 2. How it compares to the market

- **Google L6 PMs:** On Levels.fyi, Google PM pay rises to $514,125 at L6. The middle half of L6 PMs earn roughly $419,700 to $671,136. Your $552K average is a little above the median, not near the top.
- **Base salary:** $235K is just above the midpoint ($227K) of the posted $183K–$271K range, so there's room to go up.
- **Meta IC6 PMs:** This is the comparison that matters most. Levels.fyi data from October 2026 puts L5 at $410K, L6 at $612K for Meta PMs. Meta's IC6 corresponds to Google's L6, so a typical IC6 PM at Meta already earns more than this offer averages. Meta also gives annual RSU refresher grants in February, also vesting quarterly over 4 years. If you've been at Meta a few years, those refreshes have stacked up, and your current pay probably won't drop off the way this offer does in years 3–4.

## 3. What leaving would cost you

- **Unvested Meta stock** that you'd give up.
- **Your Meta February refresh grant**, if you leave before it's awarded.
- **Your 2026 annual bonus**, if Meta pays it after you'd leave. Check your payout date. If the bonus pays in Q1 and you leave in Q4, you could lose most of a year's bonus.

The offer has no sign-on bonus, so nothing currently covers any of this.

## 4. My recommendation: negotiate, and be ready to walk away

Before you reply, write down your actual Meta pay for the next 12 months: base, target bonus, and stock vesting from all your grants. Then use this rule: **move only if Google's 4-year average (without counting refreshes) beats your Meta run-rate by about 15% or more.** You're happy where you are, so the switch needs a real premium to cover the risk of a new team and of refreshes being uncertain.

**What to ask for:**

| Item | Current | Ask | Realistic landing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base | $235K | **$265K** (near the top of the posted range) | $250–260K |
| GSUs | $1.08M | **$1.4–1.5M** | $1.25–1.35M |
| Sign-on | $0 | **$100–150K**, tied to your forfeited bonus and stock | $50–100K |

Stock is usually the most flexible part of a Google offer. The posted range caps base salary, and sign-on bonuses are usually tied to what you're giving up.

At about $255K base, a $1.3M grant and a $75K sign-on, the offer works out to roughly **$875K in year 1 and a $650K average**. That's well above the Google L6 median and likely competitive with a strong Meta IC6 package.

**How to frame it to the recruiter:** "I wasn't looking and I'm happy at Meta. To move, I need a package that clearly beats what I'd earn by staying, including my Meta refreshes and the [$X] I'd give up in unvested stock and bonus. If you can get to [base / GSU / sign-on], I'm ready to sign." Share your current numbers if they help your case, and send proof (offer letter, vesting schedule) if asked.

**Walk away if** Google can't get to a 4-year average that clearly beats your Meta run-rate. You lose nothing by staying.

If you share your current Meta base, bonus target and stock vesting schedule, I can run the exact side-by-side comparison and work out your minimum acceptable number.
